entries.title: TikTok agrees to pay $400m to settle US children's privacy case
entries.summary: The US Justice Department sued TikTok in 2024 over allegations that it violated children's online privacy laws. The settlement is believed to be one of the largest ever over the issue.
entries.content:
August 22, 2026

The US Justice Department sued TikTok in 2024 over allegations that it violated children's online privacy laws. The settlement is believed to be one of the largest ever over the issue.

TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance agreed on Friday to pay $400 million (roughly €342 million) to resolve allegations by the US Justice Department that the platform violated children's online privacy laws.

"Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly," the department said in a statement.

It's "one of the largest recoveries ever obtained" from a case involving the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), a federal law which safeguards online privacy of minors, the statement added. 

What was TikTok accused of?

The Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission sued TikTok and ByteDance in 2024, alleging that the platform put children's privacy at risk.

The agencies accused TikTok of knowingly allowing children to use the platform and violating federal law that online services directed at children obtain parental consent before collecting their personal data.

The Justice Department said that since the lawsuit was filed, TikTok has "undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions and privacy practices" concerning younger users.

TikTok parent company ByteDance sold off a majority stake of its US entity earlier this year in order to avoid a ban by the Trump administration.

TikTok did not immediately comment on the settlement.

TikTok faces growing global scrutiny

The settlement comes as TikTok, alongside other social media platforms, faces increasing pressure around the world.

In 2024, Brussels launched a probe into TikTok under the Digital Services Act (DSA) — a landmark regulation that the European Union has used to curb harmful practices by Big Tech in recent years.

The video-sharing platform risks a large fine after the EU accused TikTok in July of failing to protect children through account settings that can expose them to risks such as  "unwanted contact, cyberbullying, or predatory behavior."

The United Kingdom also launched a probe into TikTok in July to investigate whether the app is doing enough under UK law to protect children from harmful content. 

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Sweden: One killed in school sword attack
entries.summary: Police have said they have arrested an individual who stabbed several people, killing one person, with a sword at a high school in central Sweden.
entries.content:
Published August 21, 2026last updated August 21, 2026

Police have said they have arrested an individual who stabbed several people, killing one person, with a sword at a high school in central Sweden.

A person armed with a sword has wounded multiple people at a school in Fagersta in central Sweden, authorities said Friday.

Police said one person had been taken into custody and there was no longer any danger to the public.

After initially saying three people had been wounded in the attack, two of them severely, police later said an additional person had been killed.

Earlier on Friday, Sweden's healthcare authority said two boys, both aged between 12 and 17, were being treated in hospital.

Police said the suspect was an 18-year-old man, whom they shot during a confrontation and took into custody.

What else do we know?

Police were called to the Brinellskola, a secondary school in Fagersta, at around 2 p.m. local time (1200 GMT). The school, which has some 450 students aged 16 to 20, had just reopened after the summer holidays.

Public broadcaster SVT reported that ambulances, police cars and a police helicopter were outside the property.

The municipality said other schools and some public buildings in the area had been locked down.

Fagersta, home to some 12,000 people, lies around 170 kilometers (105 miles) northwest of the capital, Stockholm.

Reactions to 'terrible news'

"Our thoughts are with all those affected," Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said in a post on X. "We do not yet know what lies behind the act, but we know that the police are working very intensively."

Magdalena Andersson, leader of the opposition Social Democrats, lamented the "terrible news."

"When violence takes place at a school, I know it impacts everyone in our country. All of Sweden ⁠stands together with Fagersta at this difficult time," she wrote on X.

Other attacks at educational institutions

Sweden has seen a number of high-profile attacks at educational facilities in recent years.

In February 2025, a 35-year-old man killed 10 people at an adult education center in Orebro.

In another incident, an 18-year-old student fatally stabbed two teachers at a Malmo high school in March 2022.

entries.title: 'Masha and the Bear': Ukraine sanctions Russian cartoon
entries.summary: Ukraine has imposed sanctions on the hit Russian children's cartoon "Masha and the Bear," a step towards banning it. The culture minister called the show propaganda. Russia said the move showed Kyiv's "ugly nature."
entries.content:
Ukraine

'Masha and the Bear': Ukraine sanctions Russian cartoon

August 21, 2026

Ukraine has imposed sanctions on the hit Russian children's cartoon "Masha and the Bear," a step towards banning it. The culture minister called the show propaganda. Russia said the move showed Kyiv's "ugly nature."

Ukrainian Culture Minister Tetyana Berezhna on Friday said Kyiv had imposed sanctions on the "producers and distributors" of the Russian children's cartoon series "Masha and the Bear," or "Masha i Medved" in the original language. 

The step will enable Kyiv to seek to remove and demonentize the series on websites like YouTube or streaming services like Netflix in the country. 

The cartoon about a mischievous young girl's unlikely friendship and adventures with a retired circus bear, loosely based on a Russian oral fairytale of the same name, launched in 2009 and quickly became one of Russia's most successful televisual exports. 

What did the government in Kyiv say about the sanctions?

"Ukraine has imposed sanctions against the producers and distributors of the Russian animated series Masha and the Bear," Berezhna said on social media. "This creates legal grounds to block the content in Ukraine and engage international platforms to restrict its monetization and distribution."

The show has also faced criticism from allies of Ukraine like Estonia and the UK for allegedly painting Russia in a positive light or for military or Soviet symbols sometimes appearing in the show.

"Russian propaganda has no place on children's screens — in Ukraine or anywhere in the world," Berezhna said.

In further comments on Facebook, Berezhna said the Ukrainian language channel for the show had 800 million views in 2025 alone. The Ukrainian language channel currently has roughly 18 million subscribers.

Worldwide, as of June 2026, the show had more than 54 billion combined views on YouTube, making it one of the 50 most popular feeds on the entire site.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree imposing sanctions on the creators of the show for spreading "pro-Russia narratives" and for posing a threat to Ukrainian national security. They target the studio, the show's founder, and the series' scriptwriter and director.

Ukraine said it would seek to have its sanctions mirrored by international partners, potentially widening the restrictions.

How did the show's makers and the Russian government respond?

The company behind the show, Animaccord Animation Studios, has called past allegations that the show contains Russian propaganda "false and defamatory," saying that it operates independently and receives no funding from the government in Moscow.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked about the sanctions on Friday and said that the cartoon series had "conquered the world" by promoting "the finest human qualities."

"The fact that Ukraine has launched a war against cartoons, too, likely serves as yet another illustration of the ugly nature" of the authorities in Kyiv, he said.

Is 'Masha and the Bear' controversial, and why?

The show has been on the radar of Ukrainian authorities for almost a decade. The first complaint by the State Film Agency dates back to 2017, amid the illegal annexation of Crimea and the lower-level war in Ukraine waged by separatists supported by Russia. Since the 2022 full-scale invasion the issue has come into sharper focus still.

In June, Kyiv protested against streaming giant Netflix's move to acquire the rights to stream new seasons of "Masha and the Bear."

A group of more than 50 British parliamentarians this year appealed to Culture Minister Lisa Nandy to urge streaming platforms to remove the cartoon. They argued that some episodes exposed children to Russian and Soviet military imagery.

Several Estonian politicians have also argued that "Masha and the Bear" is an instrument of Russian soft power, not least because of the several amiable bears in its cast.

Some Western analysts have warned against exaggerating these fears, though — for instance UK academic Mark Galeotti, who wrote an article objecting to the British lawmakers' appeal in July, saying the show was not "the most elevated of television," but "it is cute and it has a big heart."

In its earlier days, "Masha i Medved" was also a topic of some controversy in Russia. It sometimes drew critical comparisons to Western children's shows and prompted debate on whether it was contradicting traditional values about the roles of girls and fathers in Russian society, given Masha's mischievous nature and her paternal bear's gentle use of positive reinforcement rather than correctional discipline.

entries.title: German army helps Poland construct a defensive barrier against Russia
entries.summary: Poland is building a defense system along its northern and eastern borders to protect itself from Russia. Since June, German sappers have been assisting their NATO ally with the construction of the East Shield.
entries.content:
Poland

German army helps Poland protect itself against Russia

August 21, 2026

Poland is building a defense system along its northern and eastern borders to protect itself from Russia. Since June, German sappers have been assisting their NATO ally with the construction of the East Shield.

Poland started to construct a defensive barrier along its border with Russia and Belarus in 2024. The East Shield defense system will eventually be around 800 kilometers long, and is intended to protect this country on NATO's eastern flank against attack from the east.

When the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, inspected the first completed section in November 2024, he declared that the project was meant to "deter and discourage a potential aggressor" and was "truly an investment in peace."

The Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 was a profound shock to Poland's sense of security. The Tusk government has increased defense spending in 2026 to 200 billion zlotys (around 46 billion euros, or 54 billion dollars) ― almost 5% of Poland's GDP. This means that, in relative terms, Poland has the highest defense spending of all the members of NATO. The government has also bought the most advanced weapons available, particularly from the US, and is proceeding with the construction of the East Shield, a complex defense system along its eastern border.

A shield against Russia

Since June, around 40 German sappers, or combat engineers, have been helping to establish the defenses. The German army's combat engineer unit is specially trained in blocking the movement of enemy troops. The sappers are currently deployed near Budry in Masuria, close to the border with Russia. The fence marking the border is visible from where they are working, partially obscured by a row of trees on the Polish side.

The German soldiers are installing anti-tank obstacles to impede battle tanks in the event of an attack. A yellow backhoe loader lifts the spiky concrete blocks, known as Czech hedgehogs, off a truck and places them on the muddy ground.

This installation, around 200 meters back from the border, consists of three rows of these concrete blocks. A deep ditch and another line of hedgehogs run along the border itself. A Polish officer explains that mines can quickly be laid in the zone between the two lines of Czech hedgehogs.

"The German sappers have done an excellent job," the Polish general Stanislaw Czosnek said when he inspected the works on Thursday. He added that he was "very impressed" by his German colleagues' performance.

In the six weeks since their deployment, the German engineers have laid more than a kilometer of blocks.

"We stand ready to fight for democracy and freedom," stressed the German general Tito Gante, who accompanied Czosnek on the inspection. He praised the comradely atmosphere between the German and the Polish soldiers.

The Bundeswehr has declared its support for the East Shield an official mission: "We want to maintain peace with a credible deterrent," Gante said.

The German contingent will stay until October, but the sappers will soon be deployed at other sections of the East Shield. The work near Budry is due to be completed over the coming week.

Politically symbolic

"Above all, the participation of German sappers has politically symbolic significance," Lukasz Jasinski, an analyst at the Polish Institute for International Affairs, told DW. "Poland wants to convince Germany and other partners that Poland's eastern border is also the external border of the EU and NATO. Our Western partners should treat this border a bit like their own."

Poland and Germany were quick to establish military cooperation after the end of the Cold War. Later, when Poland joined NATO in 1999, this created the necessary political and institutional conditions for close collaboration. Since then, NATO's Multinational Corps Northeast, in which Poland and Germany both have leading roles, has been headquartered in the Polish city of Szczecin.

In 2003, Germany sold the MiG-29 fighter jets it inherited from the former East German Air Force to Poland for the symbolic price of one euro each. Joint military exercises and exchange programs for both officers and soldiers are now standard practice.

When Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, there were initial tensions between Germany and Poland on account of the cautious response from Berlin. Overall, though, the attack has further strengthened cooperation between the two. The Bundeswehr has supported Polish air defense by supplying several units of the Patriot air defense system, with their German crews. German fighter jets are helping to protect Polish air space, most recently as part of the NATO mission Enhanced Air Policing North (eAPN) in Malbork.

Questions of military cooperation were also prioritized in the closing statement that followed German-Polish intergovernmental consultations on December 1, 2025. The process culminated in the signing of the German-Polish defense agreement on June 17, 2026.

On August 15 this year, three German planes, two Eurofighters and an A400M transport aircraft, participated in the celebration of Polish Armed Forces Day. The head of the German air force, Holger Neumann, was one of the guests of honor. Some American GIs marched in the military parade ― but no German soldiers.

Kaczynski: No German soldiers in Poland

However, not all the political forces in Poland are happy about this new Polish-German brotherhood-in-arms. Memories of the trauma of World War II are still very much alive in Polish society and are regularly instrumentalized by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) to stir up anti-German feeling.

Back in 2014, PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski said he didn't want any German soldiers in Poland.

"It will be at least seven generations before that is acceptable," he said.

In the fall of 2022, when the German government offered to relocate two German Patriot batteries to Poland after an incident involving a Ukrainian rocket gone astray, the PiS government blocked the move.

"Germany's previous behavior gives us no reason to believe that it will decide to fire on the Russian rockets," Kaczynski declared.

Just last March, Poland's president Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, vetoed legislation that would have allowed Poland to access almost 44 billion euros (55 billion dollars) in EU defense loans because German armaments companies could also have benefited.

Poland sees the US as the most important guarantor of its security, and is trying to establish a special relationship with Washington. Around 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in various places around the country. Warsaw is keen to establish a permanent military base on its territory: Until now, a significant number of the US soldiers are in Poland on rotation.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: France issues warning over thousands of substandard condoms
entries.summary: French anti-fraud and health agencies have issued a recall order for roughly 260,000 condoms. They advised users to consider sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy tests amid risks of bursting or perforations.
entries.content:
August 21, 2026

French anti-fraud and health agencies have issued a recall order for roughly 260,000 condoms. They advised users to consider sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy tests amid risks of bursting or perforations.

France's anti-fraud and health agencies issued a joint statement on Friday saying they were recalling more than a quarter of a million condoms that could be defective. 

It said that the majority were sold online via major marketplaces by Asian vendors.

What did the government agencies say about the potentially substandard condoms?

Of the roughly 260,000 contraceptives being recalled, authorities said around 1,000 boxes, or 40,000 individual condoms, had already been sold. 

"Laboratory analyses identified two non-compliant products, characterized by a risk of bursting and, in one case, the presence of perforations," authorities said.

The anti-fraud agency, the DGCCRF, and the DGS health agency said in a joint statement that the condoms lacked the required CE marking that designates a product conforms with the standards of the European Economic Area trading zone. 

"The identified condoms lack a CE marking, third-party conformity assessment, and — in most cases — packaging in French," the government agencies said. "Consequently, they are deemed non-compliant and potentially pose serious risks to user health and safety (such as sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancies)."

The statement advised people who had used the condoms to get screened for sexually transmitted infections and to take a pregnancy test if they had any reason to be suspicious such as a missed or late period. 

The government said the online vendors had agreed to remove the affected listings and to send in the recalled products.

The statement listed two brands of condoms made by a Japanese company, Okamoto Industries, and the brands MyLubie and Friday Bae by Passage du Desir.

France offers people aged up to 25 free condoms via pharmacies without a prescription in a bid to prevent STIs and unwanted pregnancies.

entries.title: Iran's president: Time to end war in 'position of strength'
entries.summary: Iranian media cite Masoud Pezeshkian as saying it would be a good time to end the war with the US, "as we are in a position of strength and dignity." He also said Tehran would never "bow to intimidation."
entries.content:
Iran

Iran's president: Time to end war in 'position of strength'

August 21, 2026

Iranian media cite Masoud Pezeshkian as saying it would be a good time to end the war with the US, "as we are in a position of strength and dignity." He also said Tehran would never "bow to intimidation."

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday that it would be an opportune moment to seek to end the war with the United States, according to state media reports. 

His comments, made at a medical conference, come amid mixed messages both from officials in Tehran and from US President Donald Trump on the conflict. The partial truce agreed in June remains in a seemingly ambiguous state, having expired without progress or renewal on Monday. 

Tehran continues to severely limit shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the United States is in turn trying to enforce what it refers to as a blockade of Iran's ports. 

Trump this week threatened increased economic pressure on Iran. But how much further the US can turn the screws on one of the world's most heavily sanctioned countries, with which it does almost no business, is unclear.

As Pezeshkian seemingly suggested it might be a good time to negotiate peace, an Iranian military leader threatened "crushing, punishing and devastating responses" if the US did try to isolate Iran further economically.

What did Pezeshkian reportedly say?

According to IRNA's report, Pezeshkian said the war would eventually have to be brought to an end.

"It is better to end it today, as we are in a position of strength and dignity," he said.

"The whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America has attacked our schools, hospitals and infrastructure in violation of all regulations and is hated around the world," Pezeshkian said.

He also argued that the faltering 15-point Memorandum of Understanding signed by Iran and the US in June in no way signaled a defeat for Iran. 

"They cannot find even a single clause in this commitment that indicates capitulation," he said. "All the commitments concern the other side."

While most concern the US, a minority of the 15 commitments do put the onus on Iran, although Tehran might argue they only constitute agreeing to return to the situation that existed before the war. The most notable examples would be allowing commercial transit without charge through the Strait of Hormuz, at least temporarily, and Iran reaffirming that it would not procure or develop nuclear weapons.

Pezeshkian also reportedly told the crowd of doctors that "under no circumstances will we bow to intimidation" and that if necessary, Iran would resist "until our last breath."

What US messaging coincides with these comments?

US President Donald Trump, after a few days dominated more by his comments on the Korean Peninsula and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, briefly returned his attention to Iran late on Wednesday.

He threatened what he referred to as the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against another country," feeling the need to write the phrase entirely in capital letters. He also referred to it as an "economic D-Day."

The message did very little to explain how the US planned to further turn the screws on Iran — which has withstood around half a century of US sanctions and does almost no trade with the US — except to say the US would look to stop Iran's trading partners from providing "any type of lifeline to Iran."

Asked to shed more light on the idea in a CNBC interview on Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed it would be the "greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world," and said it would "collapse this regime."

The economic pressure would make "large-scale" military operations unnecessary, he added.

When asked if China, Iran's most important trading partner would be asked to join in, Bessent declined to comment publicly.

What other comments are coming out of Tehran?

Not unlike the volatile US president, Iran is known for its often inconsistent and hyperbolic messaging, frequently combining apparent overtures for peace and threats on the same day or even in the same message.

It's also fairly common for the Tehran regime's political representatives like Pezeshkian and lead negotiator Mohammad Qalibaf to adopt a slightly more diplomatic posture than the military or theocratic leaders.

The chief of Iran's armed forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi, was also asked about the US economic threats on Friday and warned of a broad and decisive military response if necessary.

"With preparedness across land, sea, air, air defense and cyberspace, Iran's armed forces will respond to the enemy's new threats with crushing, punishing and devastating responses," Abdollahi was quoted as saying.

Meanwhile, chief negotiator and parliamentary speaker Qalibaf seemed to voice a similar call to intensify negotiations, claiming that Washington appeared to have concluded it could not prevail in a direct military confrontation.

"We must make plans to deal with the unjust sanctions so we can overcome them," Qalibaf said in neighboring Iraq.

entries.title: 40 years after the Lake Nyos disaster in Cameroon
entries.summary: On August 21, 1986, a silent cloud of carbon dioxide swept through villages around Lake Nyos in Cameroon, killing nearly 2,000 people in their sleep. Four decades later, survivors are still living with the trauma.
entries.content:
August 21, 2026

On August 21, 1986, a silent cloud of carbon dioxide swept through villages around Lake Nyos in Cameroon, killing nearly 2,000 people in their sleep. Four decades later, survivors are still living with the trauma.

"The Lake Nyos disaster took everybody by surprise. We had no warning signals before it ever took place," said Isaac Konfor Njilah, a Cameroonian geologist and head of a laboratory in the department of Earth Sciences at the University of Yaounde.

On the night of August 21, 1986, Lake Nyos suddenly released a massive cloud of carbon dioxide that spread through nearby valleys and villages. The gas replaced oxygen, suffocating people and animals as they slept.

Located in Cameroon's Northwest Region, about 315 kilometers (196 miles) northwest of Yaounde, Lake Nyos sits inside an ancient volcanic crater in the Oku volcanic field. At the time of the incident, the area's population exceeded 3,000, with many families relying on farming and cattle ranching.

The disaster claimed the lives of about 1,700 people and some 3,500 head of livestock, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in Cameroon's history.

How did a lake become deadly?

Following the disaster, scientists from Cameroon and abroad launched extensive investigations to determine what had happened.

They concluded that carbon dioxide from deep underground had been accumulating at the bottom of the lake for years, trapped beneath more than 200 meters (656 feet) of water.

Before the disaster, the upper layers of the lake contained oxygen-rich water, while the deeper layers were saturated with dissolved carbon dioxide. Njilah explains that water has an insatiable appetite for carbon dioxide.

"So when carbon dioxide comes from the [Earth's] mantle, it is being dissolved continuously in the lake," Njilah told DW.

Scientists often compare Lake Nyos to a giant bottle of carbonated water. For decades, carbon dioxide built up in the lake's depths. When that balance was disturbed, the gas escaped in a rapid chain reaction, releasing a deadly cloud that rolled through nearby communities.

Researchers believe a landslide may have triggered the release by disturbing the gas-rich waters at the bottom of the lake.

Carbon dioxide is harmless at normal atmospheric levels. But in high concentrations, it acts as an asphyxiant, displacing oxygen in the air. Because the gas is heavier than air, it flowed downhill into villages, where many residents died in their sleep before realizing anything was wrong.

Tragedy at another lake in Cameroon just two years prior

The Nyos tragedy was not a first in Cameroon. Two years earlier, on August 15, 1984, a similar event occurred at nearby Lake Monoun, about 100 kilometers southeast of Nyos. A sudden release of carbon dioxide killed 37 people.

Scientists were still investigating the Monoun disaster when the far deadlier catastrophe struck at Lake Nyos. Researchers eventually concluded that the deaths were caused by a rare phenomenon known as a limnic eruption, in which gas-rich deep waters suddenly rise to the surface and release dissolved gases.

In the years that followed, engineers installed degassing pipes in Lake Nyos to gradually release carbon dioxide trapped deep below the surface.

Today, Njilah says the lake no longer contains enough dissolved carbon dioxide to trigger a disaster.

"The lake is very safe for the population to return," he told DW.

Survivors still live with the trauma

For survivors, however, the fear remains. Tsang Emelda Njah was just 5 years old when the disaster happened.

"We were at home, and there was a big vibration of the house," she recalled. "We thought it was just the house that was about to collapse. But we were not sure what it was. So we ran out."

Kum Samuel, who was 17 at the time, returned to his village and was confronted with a scene of pure horror.

"I saw my parents lying there dead. Chickens, flies and birds. Dogs together with our elders. I wasn't sure what to do."

For Ndong Frederick Bah, the losses were deeply personal.

"Nine of us went to bed that night, and I was the lone survivor of the family," he told DW, adding that the next day, people who had heard about the disaster came and rescued him.

Entire communities were later relocated to new settlements. Although scientists have reduced the risk of another gas release, many survivors still struggle to overcome the trauma.

"I am a child of Nyos," said Tsang Emelda Njah. "But I am still afraid to go close to the lake. That's because whatever killed people there, I am not sure whether or not it has been stopped from ever happening again. That is why we are still afraid."

Anglophone crisis harms restoration

While scientists consider the lake safe, long-term reconstruction efforts have been slowed by Cameroon's Anglophone crisis.

The conflict erupted in 2016 between government forces and separatist groups in the country's primarily English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions, where Lake Nyos is located.

According to Njilah, plans to rehabilitate affected communities and encourage people to return to their ancestral lands have been disrupted by insecurity, with the area now difficult to access.

"It is the plight of the survivors to go back home. They want to go back to their ancestral land so that they are able to pour libations on the graves of their forefathers," he said.

The ongoing violence has also hindered scientific work and development projects.

"Nobody can venture [there,] unless you want to have a bullet lodged in your head," Njilah said. "It has affected government and international agencies who are working there."

Blaise Eyong contributed reporting.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Ukraine's farmers struggle to sell harvest amid war, drought
entries.summary: Russian attacks on ships and ports in the Black Sea are threatening Ukraine's agricultural sector. Grain exports are severely restricted, and Kyiv is seeking solutions.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine's farmers struggle to sell harvest amid war, drought

August 21, 2026

Russian attacks on ships and ports in the Black Sea are threatening Ukraine's agricultural sector. Grain exports are severely restricted, and Kyiv is seeking solutions.

Russian attacks on civilian ships have effectively brought the ports in the greater region of Odesa to a standstill. Until recently, they handled about 90% of Ukraine's agricultural exports.

The Ukrainian government has been working on finding alternative routes via rail, road and other waterways. It is also currently in negotiations about an export corridor that would go via Moldova.

But many experts have pointed out that these temporary alternatives cannot replace the ports, and warn that the current blockade of the Black Sea is an even greater threat to the Ukrainian economy than that posed by Russia's full-scale invasion of 2022.

The strained security situation in the Black Sea is already having a palpable effect on Ukraine's domestic market. According to Denys Marchuk, the deputy chairman of the All-Ukrainian Agrarian Council, Ukrainian farmers have already harvested more than 28 million tons of grains and pulses.

But a large part of this harvest cannot be sold, which has led to a shortage of the cash needed to complete the harvest and to plant winter crops. Planting usually begins at the end of August in Ukraine's southern regions.

"Right now, we can barely sell our harvest. Instead, we're storing what we have harvested — that's if we find storage space. At the same time, we are wondering what to do because we need money, especially so we can plant in fall," Marchuk told DW.

He predicted that the situation would continue to worsen in the coming weeks and months when grain and oilseed crops, which are usually harvested later, compounded the crisis.

Farmers plan to leave corn in the fields

The corn harvest alone could reach about 33 million metric tons this year. Yet in the coming months, there could be a shortage of storage capacity totaling up to 10 million tons. Regions on the front, where most silos have been destroyed amid the ongoing war, are particularly affected.

"You often hear that farmers want to leave their corn in the fields to be harvested in spring. It still needs to be dried, which needs a lot of electricity that is very expensive. They don't have the money," said Marchuk. "There aren't enough places where they can sell it, nor are the prices reasonable, so for them it makes more sense to leave it in the fields as that's cheaper."

Domestic prices falling

Maksym Hopka, an analyst at the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club, estimates that Ukraine's agricultural output totaled about 3.7 million metric tons in July, of which about 2.7 million metric tons comprised grain. That was a decline of about a quarter in comparison to the previous month. He expected an additional fall of over 50% in August.

Hopka added that domestic prices were falling, with the price of food-grade wheat declining by 30 to 35%. This meant increasingly difficult economic conditions for production, he explained.

Prices have fallen so sharply because farmers cannot export all of their harvest, and can no longer cover even their production costs.

Some farms are already operating at a loss. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, annual losses from unsold agricultural produce could amount to approximately $20.5 billion (approx. €18 billion).

Ukrainian government vows to provide support

The Ukrainian government has insisted it will do everything in its power to find new ways to export Ukrainian agricultural produce by rail or road through neighboring countries or through ports on the Danube.

However, extreme heat and drought have severely reduced the Danube's transport capacity and are also hampering Ukrainian exports. There are also problems with rail and road transport. European railways are already operating at full capacity during harvest season, and transporting large quantities of grain by road is expensive.

For Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky, the top priority remains restoring safe shipping routes to the ports in the Odesa region with the help of Ukraine's military and those of its partners. He told DW that there was no comparable medium-term alternative and that rail connections and dry ports could only serve as temporary measures until the Black Sea ports reopened.

Less help from EU than in 2022

Oleg Nivievskyi from the Kyiv School of Economics said Ukraine today had fewer ways of offsetting losses in maritime trade than it did at the beginning of the full-scale invasion. In 2022, the European Union provided support to Ukraine by establishing "solidarity lanes," and import duties and quotas were temporarily suspended to ease trade.

Nivievskyi pointed out that the conditions were different now. "If we look at trade with the EU, we have gone from a free system to the pre-war trade regime with customs restrictions and quotas," he said.

He added that there were also significant shortcomings in the infrastructure, with the Ukrainian railway currently running 30% fewer trains than before 2022. Russia's constant attacks on rail infrastructure have hampered operations and necessitated regular repairs. Transport via road is also limited due to shortage of truck drivers, not least because many had been mobilized to fight in the war.

Export strategies need rethink

Nivievskyi said the current crisis could help to encourage the government to rethink Ukraine's export policies. He said the country should have developed a long-term strategy right from the beginning of the Russian invasion in order to ensure that its exports could reach global markets.

He explained it wasn't only a question of finding temporary alternatives to the ports of Odesa; the government needed to put in place logistics to ensure that the blockade of one route did not paralyze the entire sector.

Hopka has calculated that Ukraine's exports of agricultural produce will drop by about 9 million metric tons between August and October, and that losses could amount to about $1.9 billion.

In response to pressure from farmers, the government has already extended a loan program to farmers and has also applied for €220 million in aid from the European Commission. The idea is to help small and medium-sized agricultural businesses in particular to cover their payments.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

entries.title: What to do when wildfires trigger trauma
entries.summary: The wildfires this summer have broken records in Germany and are unlikely to subside in future. Psychologists say post-traumatic stress disorder caused by such disasters is serious but can be treated if people seek help.
entries.content:
Germany

What to do when wildfires trigger trauma

August 21, 2026

The wildfires this summer have broken records in Germany and are unlikely to subside in future. Psychologists say post-traumatic stress disorder caused by such disasters is serious but can be treated if people seek help.

This year, wildfires have already burned more land than the annual average from 2006 to 2025 in Germany.  North Rhine-Westphalia, the country's most populous state, has just seen the largest recorded wildfire in its history. It destroyed or damaged about 300 to 400 hectares in the Hürtgen Forest in the Eifel region.

After weeks without rain, the wildfire spread rapidly across the arid landscape with wind driving the flames in different directions. Unexploded munitions from World War II that were at risk of exploding or did explode complicated the firefighting efforts. Around 1,500 firefighters battled the flames for almost a week until the fire was stabilized, with some working 12-hour shifts.

Peter Berndgen, a spokesperson for the volunteer fire department in the Düren district in the west of the state, said that the physical and mental strain was enormous.

"Your eyes itch every night, your nose is always black and the airways and lungs are under pressure. During a 12-hour-shift, you're constantly on high alert, ready for whatever might happen," he said.

This can be trees falling or the flames changing direction, he added.

And on top of that, the constant fear that "the situation is spiraling out of my control, we won't be able to cope, you get that kind of feeling sometimes. And then you start wondering whether you'll manage to get it under control at all."

Not everyone suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder

Despite being prepared and professional, firefighters know they are also at risk of death. "The fear, or dread, that you can have is really, where can I take refuge, how will I get out of this. I'm right in the middle of a forest."

Andreas Meyer, a psychiatrist from the Central Institute of Mental Health in Mannheim who co-authored the "Berlin Declaration on Climate Change and Mental Health," says such situations can have long-lasting effects.

"Not everyone, but several people who experience something like this end up developing what is known as post-traumatic stress disorder. They find themselves reliving the event over and over, having nightmares, and experiencing flashbacks. Post-traumatic stress disorder is three times more common among firefighters than it is in the general population."

A typical symptom of post-traumatic stress disorder is avoidance behavior. People might avoid places that resemble those where the trauma first occurred, as well as conversations about the event itself.

"This can lead to the disorder setting in," said Meyer-Lindenberg.

He explained that it was totally normal to feel shaken immediately after such a disaster; to have trouble sleeping, for example, or to feel sad, but he said that if such a state persisted for more than a month and interfered with daily life, people should seek psychological help.

"The good news is that post-traumatic stress disorder can be treated very successfully with behavioral therapy," he said, adding that it resolved the disorder in two-thirds of patients.

Apart from post-traumatic stress disorder, wildfires and other such disasters can also trigger depression, anxiety disorder or addiction. Some studies have found that people are also more likely to self-harm or even commit suicide afterward.

Meyer-Lindenberg said that the number of psychiatric diagnoses is likely to double after such a disaster. "Fortunately, for many of those affected, the symptoms subside on their own. But, unfortunately, this is not always the case. Illness might still be detected years later."

Some population groups more likely to be affected, particularly women

Some groups of the population are more likely to be affected than others, studies have found. For example, children and adolescents, as well as people who are poor or who already had a mental illness. Women are also more likely to be affected than men.

While one in three people affected by a natural disaster is at risk of developing long-lasting post-traumatic stress disorder, this falls to one in 10 amid emergency responders.

Meyer-Lindenberg said that they were helped by experience, clear rules during an operation and working together as a team.

"So much depends on these factors when you are confronted with an emergency," he said. "Do I feel capable? Do I know what I have to do? Do I have colleagues, teammates I can rely on? Is there a structure in place or am I at the mercy of a situation?"

While ordinary people might be forced to stand by as their neighborhood goes up in flames, firefighters have the task of putting out the fire.

Peter Berndgen said that the volunteer firefighters in the Rhine region were highly motivated. "We want to protect ourselves, the population, our villages, our homes. We want to protect all of that," he said. "And I believe that gives us energy."

He added that psychological support was on hand if necessary and that talking about experiences was a routine part of operations as well as fighting the flames.

Taking action and control can be useful in fighting feeling of helplessness

Meyer-Lindenberg said that everyone affected by a natural disaster could benefit from action and taking control of their situation if possible. He said it was useful to put in place preventative measures against fires or floods, for example. However, it was not helpful to try to toughen oneself up for a disaster or to get used to them.

"Quite the contrary: if someone has already lived through such a disaster, they are more likely to suffer psychological consequences from the next one," he said

Firefighters who are able to put out a fire, as Berndgen and his colleagues did in the Hürtgen Forest, are also less likely to suffer from long-term psychological stress. "It confirms that what we did made sense," he said.

Unfortunately, he did not feel the same during the flood in the Ahr Valley five years ago, he said. "People from the Ahr region whose lives were in danger called us for help, but we knew we couldn't help them."

That is the worst possible situation for a firefighter, he said. "If I knew that I'd have to do this every six months, I would probably reach a point and ask whether I could really cope."

This article was originally published in German

entries.title: Swiss tourist jailed in Bali for insulting Hindu holiday
entries.summary: The 26-year-old was given a one-year prison sentence for offensive remarks posted on Instagram. During the trial, he apologized to the Balinese people for denigrating the Day of Silence and said he regretted his actions.
entries.content:
August 21, 2026

The 26-year-old was given a one-year prison sentence for offensive remarks posted on Instagram. During the trial, he apologized to the Balinese people for denigrating the Day of Silence and said he regretted his actions.

A Swiss man has been sentenced to one year in prison on the Indonesian resort island of Bali after insulting a sacred Hindu holiday.

A judge in the city of Denpasar found the 26-year-old guilty of making derogatory remarks on social media about the traditional "Nyepi," or Day of Silence.

On that day each year, people on the predominantly Hindu island are required to stay home and forgo work, the internet and entertainment. Streets and beaches are empty, except for special patrols tasked with ensuring that silence is observed. Even the international airport is shut down.

According to the public prosecutor's office, the Swiss tourist was informed about the Day of Silence rules by hotel staff when he arrived in Bali in February.

In video clips posted to Instagram, he boasted that he had defied the restrictions and walked to a beach during the observance. He also ranted against the tradition, calling it "crazy" and using an expletive.

The man was arrested in March after the videos sparked widespread anger and complaints to police.

"What the defendant did offended the Balinese people, hurt their faith and provoked public outrage," said presiding judge Tjokorda Putra Budi Pastima. "The defendant must be held accountable for his actions."

Man apologizes, saying he was hungry

During the trial in June, the defendant told the court he did not understand the extent of the restrictions and that it was not his intention to insult the Balinese people or their holiday.

He said he made the Instagram posts while hungry and frustrated that he could not find food during the holy day.

"I deeply regret what I did. I apologize to the Balinese people," the man said.

Since his arrest, the 26-year-old has spent five months in pre-trial detention — time that will be deducted from his one-year prison term.

Authorities in Switzerland said they were providing him with consular assistance.
